newsitem.title: YEMEN: German tourists feared death in Yemen captivity.
newsitem.headline: German tourists feared death in Yemen captivity.

text.p: Seven German tourists freed by their Yemeni captors on Wednesday spent nine days held in a cave, sometimes in fear for their lives, the German ambassador said.
Helga Strachwitz, who greeted the men after they arrived at Sanaa airport on a flight from the southeastern province of Hadramaut, said they were tired and resting in their hotel rooms.
"They were fairly treated, but it seems not as guests," she told reporters outside the Taj Shiba hotel.
"They felt in captivity... the kidnappers were nice until two days ago when another group came and it was tough. It was not easy, and in some moments they felt afraid for their lives".
Strachwitz said two of the tourists fell ill during their ordeal and treated themselves with medicines they had. One had a very high fever and the other had pain in a knee.
She said she did not know when they would return home and a senior Yemeni security official said it was up to them to decide.
"They might spend a couple of days to recover and see the beauty of Sanaa," Strachwitz said.
Journalists were told to come back on Thursday to talk to the freed motorcycle tourists who rushed to their rooms to have their first showers in 10 days. Their names were not released by the embassy.
They were freed by their abductors from the Manahil tribe in Hadramaut earlier in the day. The kidnappers on Tuesday changed their minds at the last minute about releasing them.
Strachwitz said the abductors made no demands to the German government or the tourists.

The seven men, most aged between 25 and 45, were kidnapped while riding morotcycles through the Wadi al-Dabaat area, some 770 km (480 miles) east of the capital Sanaa on March 3. They included a 55-year-old man and his son, 23, she said.
Kidnapping is a common ploy in Yemen by tribesmen holding grievances against the government or foreign oil firms.
Strachwitz thanked President Ali Abdullah Saleh who personally followed the hostage saga and tribal chiefs who helped mediate the release.
A Yemeni security official said on Tuesday last-minute negotiations centred on the tribesmen's demand of a government amnesty. He declined to say whether any of the demands had been met.
Dozens of tourists, diplomats and other foreigners have been seized in recent years in Yemen, one of the Arab world's most impoverished states.
The tribesmen have tried to use the foreigners, who have included a U.S. diplomat and a Saudi ambassador, as bargaining chips.
Siege by security forces has been the usual government response.
